channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Japan's core consumer price index excluding institutional factors such as energy subsidies and education rose 3.2% in September from a year earlier, the fastest pace since October 2023, according to the Bank of Japan.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports, citing the Bank of Japan, that Japan's core consumer price index expanded 3.2% in September 2026 from the corresponding period of 2025, the fastest annual pace since October 2023, and that the index does not include institutional factors such as energy-related subsidies and education. This is one source. The headline of the article calls the measure a "trend inflation index", while the text calls it a core consumer price index excluding institutional factors, and the row does not reconcile the two names. The row does not give the August figure, the contributions of energy, food or services, or the central bank's expected decision.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports one inflation measure, not the central bank's decision or Japanese industrial data. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a core inflation rate at a three-year high affects interest-rate expectations, the yen and the cost of imported inputs for Japanese manufacturers. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, Japan is both a large manufacturing market for bonding, sealing and coating materials and a supplier of raw materials and equipment, so changes in costs and rates could reach prices and orders, while the row gives no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the Bank of Japan's next rate decision, the contribution of energy and food to the rise, and Japanese industrial production data.

MarketScreener

item.title: KPMG's 2026 Global CEO Outlook finds confidence in the global economic outlook at 65%, down from 68% a year earlier and the lowest in five years, with information security the top concern at 31%.
item.description:
Chinatimes reports that KPMG's 2026 Global CEO Outlook Survey, released on 27 October, finds CEO confidence in the global economic outlook at 65%, down from 68% in the previous year and the lowest in five years, which it attributes to geopolitics, information security risks and the global economy. Concern about information security rose to 31% from 23% and is the top concern; uncertainty about the global economy is second at 28%, up six percentage points; geopolitical instability is at 26%, up 15 points; and regulatory pressures are also at 26%, up seven points. The Times of India, citing the same survey, says 69% of CEOs in India are confident about the global economic outlook against 65% worldwide, that the same 69% of Indian CEOs expect earnings to grow by 2.5% or more over the next three years, up from 61% a year earlier, and that globally cyber and data security is the greatest threat to growth, followed by the global economic outlook, geopolitical instability and regulatory pressures. The rows do not give the number of CEOs surveyed, the countries or sectors covered, or the views of chemical or manufacturing CEOs, and they do not define how "confidence" is measured.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a sentiment survey, not investment or output. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, confidence surveys show expectations that can lag events, and decisions on spending follow orders and financing conditions as much as sentiment. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, management confidence at customers in construction and manufacturing can influence the timing of investment and projects, which feeds into demand for bonding, sealing and coating materials, and the rows give no sector figures. Points that may be worth considering include the sector splits in the full report, purchasing managers' surveys in the coming weeks, and how the German and global readings compare.

Chinatimes | The Times of India

item.title: German Chancellor Merz proposes an EU free trade agreement with the 12-nation CPTPP, which together with the EU would cover more than a third of world trade, in a speech in Singapore on 27 October.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that Chancellor Friedrich Merz is advocating an EU free trade agreement with the CPTPP, whose 12 member states have nearly 600 million people, that such an agreement would reflect the interconnected supply and production chains, and that both sides together would account for more than a third of world trade. In the long term the EU aims for a free trade agreement with ASEAN, whose 11 member states have nearly 700 million inhabitants. MarketScreener says Merz called on European and Asian middle powers to build a strategic alliance in trade, technology and security, warning that an erosion of the established global order threatens their shared interests, and named Japan, Britain, Canada and Singapore among the CPTPP members. Lianhe Zaobao says he proposed that the EU and ASEAN accelerate negotiations on free trade agreements, with bilateral agreements with willing ASEAN members as a first step if that is hard in the short term. The Jakarta Post says Singapore's Prime Minister Lawrence Wong will push for progress on an ASEAN–EU trade deal when Singapore chairs ASEAN in 2027. The Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung describes the speech as the "Singapore Lecture", the first stop of a five-day Asia trip with further stops in Tokyo and Seoul.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows describe a proposal in a speech, not a mandate or a negotiation. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, free trade agreements take years to negotiate, and the EU already has agreements with several ASEAN countries. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, tariffs, rules of origin and standards in such agreements affect the cost of raw materials and finished goods that cross borders, and a framework built around supply chains could ease sourcing in the long run, while the rows give no figures or sector terms. Points that may be worth considering include the Commission's response, any negotiating mandate, and how chemicals and product standards would be treated.

Handelsblatt | MarketScreener | Lianhe Zaobao | The Jakarta Post | Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung

item.title: China's exports to Germany rose by 31.4% in September while its imports from Germany rose by only 0.1%, Handelsblatt reports as Federal President Steinmeier starts his last visit to China in office.
item.description:
Handelsblatt reports that Federal President Frank-Walter Steinmeier began his last visit to China in office in Hefei on 27 October, that the trip is under special observation because German policy towards China has tightened significantly under Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and that in September 2026 China's exports to Germany rose by 31.4% while its imports from the Federal Republic rose by only 0.1%. The Straits Times reports that Merz, speaking in Singapore during a five-day Asia tour amid rising EU–China trade strains, said that decoupling from China would be "a big mistake", backed "de-risking and diversification", and cited a trade deficit with China that reached EUR 360 billion in 2025. The Straits Times row does not say whether that deficit is Germany's or the EU's, and it is an annual figure, so it is not comparable with the September growth rates. The Handelsblatt row does not say whether the September changes compare with a year earlier or with the previous month, whether the figures are Chinese or German data, or which products or values lie behind them. It gives no levels.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give growth rates without levels, so the size of the trade cannot be read from them. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, Chinese exports to Germany growing far faster than German exports to China could point to a widening bilateral gap, though the rows give no levels, and the mix of goods decides which German industries meet more competition. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, trade between Germany and China covers chemicals, vehicles and machinery among other goods, so a rise in Chinese exports to Germany could raise competition for German customers of bonding, sealing and coating materials, and the rows give no product breakdown. Points that may be worth considering include the levels and product split in German and Chinese customs data, the outcome of the Steinmeier visit, and any measures that follow from Merz's Asia tour.

Handelsblatt | The Straits Times

item.title: ACEA asks the EU for targeted exemptions to protect carmakers' operations in Türkiye under the proposed "Made in EU" rules, while the UK business minister says Britain and the EU are finding a way through its concerns.
item.description:
Hürriyet Daily News reports that ACEA, the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association, has called for targeted exemptions to protect European manufacturers' existing operations in Türkiye under the EU's proposed "Made in EU" rules, warning that exclusion could weaken their competitiveness. The call follows a Franco-German negotiating position that leaves Türkiye outside the proposed automotive framework while allowing for Britain's inclusion, and the row notes that the Industrial Accelerator Act, which seeks to strengthen European production against Chinese competition, has yet to be adopted. MarketScreener reports that British business minister Jonathan Reynolds said Britain and the EU were finding a way through concerns over the bloc's proposed "Made in Europe" rules, which would favour European-made goods in public procurement, auctions and subsidy schemes covering sectors including electric vehicles, batteries and other clean technologies, and that businesses are seeking greater clarity. The row says the rules pose a particular threat to the UK car industry. The two rows use different names, "Made in EU" and "Made in Europe", and are read as the same proposal. They do not give the text of the Franco-German position, the share of European content required, the Turkish plants or volumes at stake, what "finding a way through" means in practice, or a timetable for the act.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report a lobbying request and a minister's remark, not a decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, local-content rules decide whose parts count towards qualification, so where the line falls for third countries such as Türkiye and the UK decides which plants and suppliers are inside a European supply chain. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle assembly and component plants are customers for bonding, sealing and coating materials, so the treatment of plants outside the EU could change where materials are specified and from whom they are bought, and the rows give no figures. Points that may be worth considering include the texts of the Parliament and the Council, the treatment of Türkiye and the UK in them, and the local-content thresholds.

Hürriyet Daily News | MarketScreener

item.title: The US and Canada are reported to be working on a deal to ease Section 232 tariffs of 25% on autos and up to 50% on Canadian steel, while POLITICO's sources say neither side has dropped its original demands.
item.description:
MarketScreener reports, citing four Canadian and two US sources, that the US and Canada are working on a deal to ease US tariffs on Canadian steel and autos, with the talks focused on tariffs under Section 232 of US trade law, including 25% on autos and up to 50% on Canadian steel. The News International adds that the talks aim to repair relations after broader negotiations collapsed in August, and that industry insiders expect a targeted, narrowed deal rather than a comprehensive agreement. POLITICO reports that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Canadian Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc have been talking since 21 October and that a senior Canadian official calls the talks informal. POLITICO Europe reports that, according to half a dozen current and former officials, industry representatives and others, neither side has dropped its original demands: Prime Minister Mark Carney's request for lower auto tariffs and Trump's push for more access to Canada's alcohol and dairy markets. The Mainichi reports that Carney says talks have picked up slightly and that any progress is because Washington is moving closer to Canada's demands, that White House economic adviser Kevin Hassett suggested the countries are close to a deal, and that Carney cannot be sure Trump would honour a new agreement. Chinatimes quotes a Canadian source who says a deal on steel and auto tariffs is possible before 3 November, while a US source says the administration hopes Canada will make more concessions. The accounts differ on how close a deal is. The rows give no draft text, no tariff levels in a possible deal and no date for a deal beyond the 3 November possibility.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report negotiations and anonymous sources, not a decision. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, tariffs on steel and autos work through input costs and through trade between two integrated markets, and a narrow deal would change particular product lines rather than the overall tariff structure. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, automotive and steel-using manufacturing in both countries are customers for bonding, sealing and coating materials, so a change in auto tariffs could shift vehicle volumes and the cross-border sourcing of components, and the rows give no figures. Points that may be worth considering include any signed text or proclamation, whether the 25% and 50% rates change, and how a deal would interact with the tariff changes due on 30 October.

MarketScreener | The News International | POLITICO | POLITICO Europe | The Mainichi | Chinatimes | The Globe and Mail

item.title: Ifo says German industry's export expectations rose by 3.2 points to 12.2 in October, the best since the war in Ukraine began, with carmakers up from minus 15.1 in September to plus 12.7.
item.description:
Süddeutsche Zeitung, citing the Ifo Institute in Munich, reports that the export expectations of German industry are as good as they have been since the war in Ukraine began: in October they rose by 3.2 points to 12.2 points. Klaus Wohlrabe, head of Ifo surveys, says the automotive industry in particular has revised its export prospects upwards significantly: in September its expectations were clearly negative at minus 15.1 and now they are plus 12.7, which the row explains as the share of companies expecting rising exports being 12.7 percentage points higher than the share expecting falling exports. Prospects are particularly positive in beverage production, at 57.7 points, followed by data processing equipment, electrical equipment, textiles and clothing, and mechanical engineering, with values between 29.1 and 15.7 in descending order. Slightly negative export expectations exist, among others, in the chemical industry and the paper industry. This is one source. The row does not give the September level of the overall index, the number of firms surveyed, the reasons for the swing in the automotive industry, the exact values for chemicals and paper, or any export data.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports a survey of expectations, not orders or export values. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, such a balance shows how many firms plan higher or lower exports, can change quickly between months, and reaches actual volumes with a delay. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, carmakers, electrical equipment and mechanical engineering are customers for bonding, sealing and coating materials, so firmer export plans there could support demand in Germany, while slightly negative expectations in the chemical industry itself could point to a weaker view of sales abroad, and the row gives no figures for either. Points that may be worth considering include the chemical and paper readings in the full Ifo release, German export data for the coming months, and whether the automotive reading holds in the next survey.

Süddeutsche Zeitung

item.title: Top food and consumer goods firms including Nestlé, Reckitt, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola warn of further price rises next year to cover higher freight, raw material and energy costs linked to the war on Iran.
item.description:
Arab News and Yahoo report that the world's top food and consumer goods companies, including Nestlé, Reckitt, Procter & Gamble and Coca-Cola, have warned of further price rises next year to cover higher costs, while shoppers remain reluctant to spend on groceries. Both rows tie the cost increases to higher freight, raw material and energy costs resulting from the US war on Iran, and both describe a balancing act for the firms in protecting profit margins. Arab News adds that higher grocery and gas bills are a major factor in the US midterm elections next week, and Yahoo says higher prices on everyday items will fuel concerns that inflation will persist into next year. The two rows give the same account in different words and read as one report. They do not give the size or timing of the planned price rises, the product categories or regions affected, which of the three cost types weighs most, how many firms stand behind "and others", or whether the warnings come from earnings calls or other statements. They give no volume or sales figures.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows report company warnings, not price lists or sales volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, brand owners that face higher freight, raw material and energy costs tend to press on the prices of what they buy, and price rises that meet reluctant shoppers can lower volumes, which then reach the packaging and materials these firms purchase. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, food and consumer goods packaging such as labels, cartons, and flexible and rigid packs is bonded, sealed and coated, so softer volumes at brand owners could reduce demand for those materials, while cost pressure at the brand owners could show up in supplier negotiations, and the rows give no figures for packaging or chemicals. Points that may be worth considering include the size and timing of the announced price rises, the effect on grocery volumes, and the next company results of the firms named.

Arab News | Yahoo!

item.title: China's passenger-car retail sales fell 21.7% year on year to 13.33 million in January to September 2026, with September down 28%, China Daily reports, citing the China Passenger Car Association.
item.description:
China Daily reports that retail sales of passenger cars in China fell 21.7% year on year to 13.33 million vehicles in the first nine months of 2026, with September sales down 28%. The China Passenger Car Association's secretary-general, Cui Dongshu, says the association's forecasting team projects 18.5 million vehicles for 2026, about 22% below the 2025 peak of 23.74 million and below the 19.29 million recorded in 2020. For 2027 the association sees retail sales rising by up to 5%, with a central forecast of 2%, which would give about 18.87 million, still roughly one-fifth below the 2025 level. Commercial Times gives the same 2026 forecast and says 2% growth in 2027 depends on the general environment and policies changing. Cnyes, citing the association, reports that China's car imports fell 20% in January to September to 290,000 vehicles, with September imports down 49% to 21,000. The rows do not give the causes of the fall, the split between electric and combustion models, export or production figures, or the policies behind the 2027 range. The Cnyes row also gives retail figures of 29,000 for September and 280,000 for nine months, which cannot be total-market sales beside 13.33 million, so they are not used here.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The rows give an association's measured nine-month figure and its own forecasts, not production or export volumes. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, a fall of this size in a national car market lowers vehicle output for the home market, while cars built for export are counted separately and the mix between electric and combustion models changes materials use per vehicle. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, vehicle bodies, glass, interiors and battery packs are bonded, sealed and coated in assembly, so lower Chinese retail sales could reduce demand from automotive customers there, and the rows give no figures for materials. Points that may be worth considering include the association's October data, production and export figures, and the policy changes behind the 2027 range.

China Daily | Commercial Times | Cnyes

item.title: German paper mills sold 14.248 million tonnes in January to September 2026, 0.3% more than a year earlier, with domestic sales down 2.6% and foreign sales up 3.1%; production of paper, board and cardboard fell 0.1% to 14.137 million tonnes.
item.description:
The September 2026 statistical short information of Die Papierindustrie gives, for January to September 2026 against the same period of 2025: production of paper, board and cardboard in Germany of 14,137,000 tonnes, down 0.1%; total sales of German paper mills of 14,248,000 tonnes, up 0.3%; domestic sales of 6,776,000 tonnes, down 2.6%; and foreign sales of 7,472,000 tonnes, up 3.1%. This is one source, a statistics sheet, and the row carries the figures without commentary. It does not give the split between packaging grades and graphic papers, the values or prices behind the tonnes, the figure for September alone, the capacity or energy costs of the mills, or the countries that foreign sales go to. Sales in the row are higher than production, and the row does not say why.

Potential Industry Impact (AI-Assessed)

The row reports tonnes of paper, board and cardboard, not a breakdown by use. On a general reading rather than on anything in the sources, paper, board and cardboard serve packaging as well as graphic and hygiene uses, and a shift of sales from domestic to foreign buyers changes where German mills' output is taken up. On the same general reading, for adhesive technologies, paper production and packaging converting use bonding, sealing and coating materials, so lower domestic sales at mills could point to softer demand from German converters while higher foreign sales could support mill output, and the row gives no figures for adhesives. Points that may be worth considering include the split by grade in later releases, the demand of German packaging converters, and the destinations of the foreign sales.

Die Papierindustrie
